Type.evidence_source: Our research, undertaken specifically with young men who have experienced suicidal behavior and/or thinking

Area.evidence_source: Risk: In line with the literature (see, e.g., Barney et al., 2006; Biddle et al., 2004; Renaud et al., 2006), we identified an underutilization of mental health services. However, our research goes further than previous epidemiologically informed studies by addressing the underlying reasons for this lack of engagement from the perspectives of young suicidal men. In so doing, our findings highlight a pervasive understanding of current services as both stigmatized and stigmatizing, as being inadequately available to young men in need, and, where access is achieved, as lacking (at least consistently) the necessary qualities needed to provide effective care.; Recovery: The need for suicide prevention programs that reach out to young men proactively is highlighted. In this regard, services that are embedded in the local community are of particular merit for a number of reasons. They are more likely to be informal in nature, based on their association with social interaction per se (rather than interaction focused exclusively on clinical care). In addition, they are more easily and discretely accessed, increasing the likelihood of contact at the time of need and in ways that are seen to protect confidentiality.
